title: Money before 59 and a half
teaches: The ways to reach retirement-account money before 59½ without the 10 percent penalty (Roth contributions, a Roth conversion ladder, the rule of 55, 72(t) payments, 457(b) plans) and how a taxable account bridges the gap

blocks.text: The tax law gives retirement accounts their advantages on one condition: the money is for retirement, which the law defines as age 59½. Take money out of a 401(k) or a traditional IRA earlier and, on top of the ordinary income tax, you pay an additional 10 percent of the withdrawal. Take the earnings out of a Roth early and the same applies, plus income tax on those earnings.[^half]

For someone who plans to keep working to 60 or later, that is the end of the matter. For anyone who stops earlier, by choice, layoff or illness, it raises a practical question: most of their savings may be in these accounts. This lesson is about the routes to that money, all of them legal and written into the tax code, and about how to plan the years before 60 so the penalty is paid rarely or never.

One thing first: the penalty is not a disaster. Ten percent of a withdrawal in a year when the income tax on it is 10 or 12 percent makes the total about what a working couple pays on their wages. Paying it occasionally can be a reasonable choice. It just usually isn't necessary.

Roth IRA withdrawals follow an order set by law.[^roth-401k] Your contributions come out first, then any converted money, oldest first, then the earnings. Contributions can be taken out at any age, for any reason, with no tax and no penalty, since they were taxed going in. Someone who has put $7,000 a year into a Roth IRA for ten years has $70,000 they can reach at any time, whatever the account has grown to.

Converted money has its own rule. Each conversion from a pre-tax account to a Roth starts a five-year clock, counted from 1 January of the year of the conversion. Once the clock runs out, the taxable part of that conversion can be withdrawn with no penalty at any age. The earnings stay locked until 59½.

That rule makes a ladder possible. In the first year after leaving work, convert a year's spending from the 401(k) or IRA to a Roth, paying the income tax on it. Do the same the next year, and the next. Five years after the first conversion it ripens and can be spent; a year later the second; and so on, one rung a year, until 59½.

The tax on each rung is low if there is little other income that year: a married couple converting $60,000 owes $2,780 in 2026, under 5 percent. The catch is the first five years, before any rung ripens, which have to be paid for with something else. Guess first.

blocks.caption: A couple with $1.2 million in pre-tax accounts and $60,000 of Roth contributions converts a year's spending each year after stopping work, and pays for each year from ripe conversions, then Roth contributions, then a taxable account, then pre-tax money with the penalty. Real dollars, 4 percent real growth.
blocks.task: Guess, then find a taxable balance with no penalty years and one with some

blocks.text: The first five years after stopping need roughly five years of spending from outside the pre-tax accounts: a taxable account, Roth contributions, cash, or part-time pay. For a couple spending $60,000, that is about $300,000, less what the Roth contributions cover. With it, the ladder takes over in year six and no penalty is ever paid. Without it, the gap years draw pre-tax money early, and the penalty falls on every dollar.

This is why, for someone who expects to stop work well before 60, a taxable account is worth building even though it is taxed more heavily than a 401(k) in lesson 8's comparison. It buys access. The usual pattern is to fill the pre-tax accounts while working, at 22 or 24 percent saved, and build the taxable bridge alongside them.

**The rule of 55.** If you leave an employer in or after the calendar year you turn 55, you can take money from that employer's 401(k) with no penalty. It applies only to the plan of the job you left, not to IRAs or older plans, so rolling an old 401(k) into the current one before leaving can widen the door. For police, firefighters and some other public safety workers the age is 50 (or after 25 years of service in that plan).

**457(b) plans.** Many state and local government employers offer a 457(b) alongside or instead of a 401(k). Its withdrawals after leaving the job carry no 10 percent penalty at any age (except on money rolled in from a 401(k) or IRA), which makes it the most flexible pre-tax account there is.

**72(t) payments.** Section 72(t) of the tax code allows penalty-free withdrawals from an IRA at any age, as a series of substantially equal periodic payments worked out from the balance, life expectancy and an interest rate.[^sepp] The payments must continue unchanged for five years or until 59½, whichever is longer. Change them early and the penalty is charged back on every payment already taken, plus interest. It suits someone who needs a steady sum from one IRA for a known stretch, and is risky for anyone whose plans might change.
**The HSA.** Old medical receipts, from lesson 8, can be reimbursed from an HSA at any age, tax- and penalty-free.
**Exceptions.** The penalty is also waived for disability, for some medical bills, for a series of other specific events, and for heirs. None is something to plan around.

Most people who stop work in their forties or early fifties combine several of these. A common shape: live on a taxable account for the first five years while converting a year's spending each year; draw on Roth contributions if the taxable account runs low; let the ladder take over from year six; at 59½, everything is open.

Three refinements matter. Convert more than a year's spending if the low brackets have room, since the extra rungs are cheap now and may not be later (lesson 10). Watch what the conversions do to health insurance credits before 65, which can cost more than the tax itself (lesson 11). And spend the taxable account's gains with an eye on the 0 percent band from lesson 7: a couple living on $60,000 from a taxable account with half of it gain may owe no tax on the sales at all, leaving the low brackets free for conversions.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Roth contributions can be withdrawn at any age, free of tax and penalty.
Each Roth conversion can be withdrawn penalty-free five years after 1 January of its year: a ladder of conversions bridges to 59½.
The first five years after stopping need other money: a taxable account, Roth contributions or part-time pay.
The rule of 55, a 457(b) and 72(t) payments are other doors, each with its own conditions.

blocks.caption: Six questions on money before 59½
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Someone aged 45 has put $50,000 of contributions into a Roth IRA that is now worth $90,000. How much can they take out with no tax or penalty?
items.why: Contributions come out first and are always free of tax and penalty. The $40,000 of earnings is locked until 59½.

items.ask: A Roth conversion is made in March 2026. When can it be withdrawn without the 10 percent penalty?
items.why: The five-year clock starts on 1 January of the conversion year, so a 2026 conversion ripens at the start of 2031.

items.ask: Why does a conversion ladder need about five years of other money at the start?
choices: No conversion can be spent penalty-free until five years after its year
The first five conversions are taxed at 37 percent
items.why: The first rung ripens five years after it is made, so the first five years of spending must come from somewhere else.

items.ask: Who can use the rule of 55?
choices: Someone who leaves an employer in or after the year they turn 55, for that employer's plan
items.why: It applies to the 401(k) of the job left in or after the year of turning 55. IRAs are not included.

items.ask: What happens if 72(t) payments are changed before the required period ends?
choices: The 10 percent penalty is charged on every payment already taken
Nothing, if the change is small
items.why: The exception only holds if the series runs unchanged for five years or until 59½, whichever is later. Breaking it brings back the penalty on all of it.

items.ask: Which account has no early withdrawal penalty after leaving the employer, at any age?
items.why: Withdrawals from a governmental 457(b) after separation are taxed as income but carry no 10 percent penalty.

summary: **The penalty is 10 percent before 59½.** It comes on top of income tax, but paying it occasionally is not a disaster.
**Roth contributions are always free.** They come out first, at any age, with no tax or penalty.
**Conversions ripen after five years.** Each one counts from 1 January of its year, so a ladder of yearly conversions bridges to 59½.
**The first five years need other money.** About five years of spending from a taxable account, Roth contributions or work.
**Conversions in empty years are cheap.** A couple converting $60,000 with no other income owes under 5 percent.
**Other doors exist.** The rule of 55 for the last employer's plan, governmental 457(b) plans, and 72(t) payments.
**A taxable account buys access.** For anyone stopping well before 60 it is worth building alongside the pre-tax accounts.

half.title: Why 59½
half.text: The age goes back to the Keogh plans for the self-employed in 1962, and was carried into IRAs in 1974. Insurers then counted age to the nearest birthday, and 59½ is when a person starts to count as 60 that way, which is the usual explanation. The 10 percent additional tax, as the IRS calls it, has applied to IRAs since 1974 and to employer plans since 1986.

sepp.title: The three methods
sepp.text: The IRS allows three ways to set 72(t) payments: required minimum distribution (a share of the balance recomputed each year), amortization and annuitization (fixed payments). Since 2022 the interest rate used may be up to 5 percent, or 120 percent of the federal mid-term rate if that is higher. A once-only switch from a fixed method to the minimum-distribution method is allowed.

roth-401k.title: Roll a Roth 401(k) into a Roth IRA first
roth-401k.text: This ordering rule applies to Roth IRAs, not to Roth 401(k)s. An early withdrawal straight from a Roth 401(k) is split between contributions and earnings in proportion to the account's balance, so part of it is taxed and penalized. Rolling the Roth 401(k) into a Roth IRA after leaving the job puts the money under the IRA ordering rule, with contributions coming out first.
